stances.claim: When a state ratifies Unclos and chooses no tribunal, it is deemed to have chosen ad hoc Annex VII arbitration -- which is what the Philippines did

The Tribunal is composed of five members -- Wolfrum (Germany, PH-nominated), Pawlak (Poland, by ITLOS President since China abstained), Cot (France), Soons (Netherlands), and Mensah (Ghana) as presiding arbitrator
PCA is not a 'court' -- it acted as the Tribunal's Registry, the rough equivalent of the Office of the Clerk of Court of our SC; it has served as Registry in 11 of 12 Annex VII cases
Despite China's non-participation, the award binds China -- but the Tribunal has no sheriff, policeman, or soldier to enforce, and the Philippines lacks military/political/economic muscle to compel

Valderrama's email illustrates the precedent: the US refused to participate in the Nicaragua ICJ case, ignored the award, and refused negotiation -- Security Council mechanisms failed; China is doing exactly the same

On the merit, the Philippines asks the Tribunal to invalidate China's nine-dash line and to characterize disputed features as 'islands, rocks, low-tide elevations, or submerged banks' -- regardless of who owns or occupies them
A PH victory would allow exploration and development of mineral, oil, and natural resources around these features because they lie within 200 nm of Zambales and Palawan coasts entitled to EEZ or CS

China maintains 'unquestioned' ownership and sovereignty over these features under its nine-dash line, justifying its construction of lighthouses, buildings, and airports -- hence the standoff between maritime entitlements and territorial-ownership claims
As the second-largest economy, with vastly superior military, and as a permanent UNSC member with veto power, China possesses the economic, military, and political clout to back its claims

Given enforcement and standoff realities, the Philippines cannot rest on its legal laurels even after a merit win -- it must continue diplomacy, negotiation, back-door channeling, and other peaceful settlement modes

Credit for opting to arbitrate goes to President Aquino, FS Albert del Rosario, SolGen Florin Hilbay (official PH 'agent'), international counsel led by Paul Reichler (interestingly Nicaragua's lawyer against the US), and advisers Justices Carpio and Jardeleza

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban delivers a post-victory reality check on the Oct 29, 2015 Arbitral Tribunal jurisdiction award: even if the Philippines wins on the merit, it will still face two grim realities -- enforcement and standoff. Before proceeding, he corrects a 'glaring error' in media coverage: the adjudicating body is neither the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea (Itlos, based in Hamburg) nor the Permanent Court of Arbitration (PCA, based in The Hague), but an ad hoc 'Arbitral Tribunal Constituted Under Annex VII of the 1982 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea.' When a state signs/ratifies/accedes to Unclos, it must choose one of four tribunals -- Itlos, ICJ, Annex VII ad hoc arbitration, or a special tribunal -- and since the Philippines chose none, it is deemed to have chosen Annex VII. The Tribunal has five members: Judge Rudiger Wolfrum (Germany, PH-nominated); Judge Stanislaw Pawlak (Poland, named by the Itlos president after China opted not to participate); Judge Jean-Pierre Cot (France); Prof. Alfred H. A. Soons (Netherlands); and Judge Thomas A. Mensah of Ghana as presiding arbitrator. The PCA is not a 'court' -- it acts as the Tribunal's 'Registry,' the rough equivalent of the Office of the Clerk of Court of our SC, and has acted as Registry in 11 of 12 Annex VII cases. On enforcement: although the Oct 29 award holds that despite non-participation China 'is bound by any award the Tribunal issues,' the Tribunal has no power to enforce -- no sheriff, policeman, or soldier -- and the Philippines lacks the military, political, and economic muscle to compel China. Filipino international arbitrator Mario E. Valderrama, in several emails, explained the precedent: 'The US, in a dispute with Nicaragua in the International Court of Justice, already did what China is doing -- refuse to participate. And what China is expected to do -- ignore the award -- was already done by the US which even refused to negotiate with the winner, Nicaragua. Being an ICJ case, there were possible mechanisms for enforcement, including recourse to the Security Council. None succeeded.' On standoff: the Philippines essentially asks the Tribunal to invalidate China's nine-dash line as inconsistent with Unclos and to determine whether disputed maritime features are 'islands, rocks, low-tide elevations, or submerged banks,' regardless of who owns or occupies them. Specifically, Scarborough Shoal and eight Spratly features are sought to be declared 'rocks or low-tide elevations or submerged banks' generating no EEZ or continental shelf. A PH victory would allow exploration and development of mineral, oil, and natural resources around these features because they lie within 200 nautical miles of the Zambales and Palawan coasts, unquestionably entitled to EEZ or CS under Unclos. China, on the other hand, maintains these fall inside its nine-dash line and claims 'unquestioned' ownership and sovereignty, justifying its construction of lighthouses, buildings, and airports. The standoff is between the Tribunal's award of maritime entitlements and China's unresolved ownership claim. As the second-largest economy, with a far superior military and a permanent UNSC seat with veto power, China possesses the economic, military, and political clout to back its claims. Given these realities, the Philippines -- even assuming a merit win -- cannot rest on its legal laurels; it must continue diplomacy, negotiation, back-door channeling, and other peaceful settlement modes. CJ closes with the open question whether a merit win will solve the dispute or just incense China and complicate it further, and credits President Aquino, FS del Rosario, SolGen Hilbay (the official 'agent'), international counsel led by Paul Reichler (interestingly Nicaragua's lawyer against the US), and legal-team advisers Justices Carpio and Jardeleza for opting to arbitrate.
